IntroductionWildland fires (hereafter ‘fires’) are increasing in frequency, intensity and societal impact in many regions under climate warming1,2,3,4. Fires alter carbon cycling, vegetation structure and land-atmosphere feedbacks, with implications for future climate5,6,7, ecosystems8,9, air quality, human health10,11,12, infrastructure and biodiversity through complex interactions between vegetation, weather, atmospheric composition and human activity. Fire emissions degrade air quality and contribute to global mortality (e.g. 1.53M deaths per year globally13), while suppression costs and damages continue to rise in many fire-prone regions (e.g. $3B per year in the United States14).Modelling how fire regimes will evolve with climate change is increasingly important for mitigation and adaptation, yet fire modelling remains highly uncertain. The uncertainties arise from interacting processes, spanning vegetation dynamics, fuel availability and moisture, ignitions, meteorology, human activity, emissions, plume evolution, atmospheric chemistry and climate feedbacks3,8,15. Models differ substantially in how these processes are represented, ranging from process-based land surface and Earth system models to statistical and machine learning approaches. Consequently, future projections (out to the end of the century) of burned area, emissions, fire weather and smoke exposure vary widely across regions and climate scenarios.Previous reviews have examined wildfire-climate interactions, and regional16,17 or global fire trends18,19. However, rapid advances in modelling capability, Earth system coupling, observational constraints and machine learning now motivate a broader synthesis focused specifically on future fire projection pathways. Here, we review major modelling frameworks used to project future fire activity under climate change, including land surface models, Earth system models and statistical and machine learning approaches (see SI Note 1 for literature review methods). We examine how these frameworks represent fire processes and climate feedbacks, evaluate their historical performance and limitations, and synthesise their projections across regions, scenarios and modelling approaches. Despite the large uncertainties, many studies project increasing fire activity across northern extra-tropical and boreal regions. Our synthesis shows that the different modelling frameworks provide complementary strengths for distinct scientific applications, and that confidence in future projections is greatest where independent approaches converge and are supported by historical model evaluation. Finally, we outline several priorities for improving the next-generation fire-climate models.Mechanistic changes in fires under climate changeWildfires interact with climate through complex processes that involve meteorology, vegetation and atmospheric composition. Major mechanisms linking climate change and wildfire activity are summarised and illustrated in Fig. 1.Fig. 1: Climate-fire interactions.Full size imageSchematic of the numerous factors and interactions between wildfires, climate and their feedbacks.Climate controls on wildland firesClimate change influences wildfires through changes in meteorological conditions, fuel availability and ignition sources. Globally, moisture and air temperature are among the strongest climatic controls on fire occurrence as they contribute to fuel flammability20,21,22,23, although dominant drivers vary regionally (Fig. 2). Even in regions where precipitation increases, warming-driven evaporation can still reduce fuel moisture and increase fire risk23,24,25,26.Fig. 2: Global schematic of key regional wildfire drivers and how climate change is altering them.Full size imageBackground land cover types are from 2018 and derived from ESA CCI278 and Xu et al.279.Earlier spring snowmelt lengthens the seasonal drying period27,28,29 and permafrost thaw in the high north can increase soil drainage and upper-soil drying26,30,31,32,33,34. Climate-driven vegetation shifts further alter fuel structure and availability, and CO2 fertilisation enhances biomass35. Biome transitions can either suppress or enhance fire activity. For example, woody encroachment in savannas may reduce burned area36, whereas expanding taiga and increasing tree mortality in high-latitude forests may increase flammability32,37,38,39,40,41,42,43.Lightning is a climate-sensitive and spatially heterogeneous driver of fire ignition44,45,46,47,48,49, and burned area in some remote regions is particularly sensitive to changes in lightning activity3,20,21,22,23,50,51,52,53,54. Additionally, winds and terrain influence fire spread8, with atmospheric blocking events associated with persistent extreme fire weather55,56.While not a climate control, human activity can also influence fires via agricultural expansion, fire suppression, land fragmentation, accidental ignition and deforestation57,58,59,60,61,62,63,64,65. In some regions, increasing suppression efforts partially offset worsening fire weather62,63,64.When major climate forcers coincide, extreme fire weather can develop, increasing the likelihood of large and severe fires23,29,66,67. Such trends are already evident in boreal forests, the western U.S. and Australia20,32,68, with attribution studies indicating a significant climate-change contribution20,21,69,70,71.Wildland fire controls on climateWildfires influence climate through changes to vegetation, atmospheric composition and chemistry (Fig. 1). The feedback can either amplify or dampen climate change depending on ecosystem type, burn severity, optical properties of smoke, atmospheric conditions and timescale.Fires alter vegetation structure, ecosystem succession and land-atmosphere energy exchange72,73. Vegetation loss reduces evapotranspiration and latent cooling, often producing warmer and drier near-surface conditions74. Severe or frequently returning fires may additionally consume organic soils and alter ecosystem recovery pathways, promoting long-term biome shifts37,38,39,75,76,77. Such shifts may reduce flammability locally, but can weaken long-term carbon uptake and potentially convert some ecosystems from net carbon sinks to sources78,79,80,81,82,83.Fires modify atmospheric composition through emissions of greenhouse gases, aerosols and ozone precursors84, influencing tropospheric ozone formation, modifying atmospheric oxidative capacity84,85,86 and altering methane lifetime86. In peat-rich ecosystems, deep burning of organic soils additionally releases long-term carbon stores to the atmosphere87.Biomass burning (BB) aerosols, primarily black carbon and organic carbon, additionally influence climate through direct radiative effects and aerosol-cloud interactions. Their net forcing remains uncertain and depends strongly on injection height, aerosol properties, atmospheric conditions, transport and cloud interactions88,89,90,91,92,93,94,95,96,97,98. Through impacts on atmospheric circulation and precipitation, BB aerosols may influence regional hydroclimate, including possible effects on the Asian monsoon and southern African precipitation99,100,101,102,103,104,105,106,107,108.Fires lower surface albedo, via charred land surfaces109,110, as well as darkening snow and ice surfaces that receive deposition of long-range transported smoke88,92,109,111,112,113. However, severe stand-replacing fires can increase winter albedo by exposing snow and reducing canopy masking75,76,79,114,115,116.These coupled feedbacks highlight the complexity of wildfire-climate interactions and the difficulty of representing them comprehensively in models3.Overview of fire modelling frameworksWildfire projections are generated using three broad modelling approaches: land surface models (LSMs), Earth system models (ESMs) and statistical or machine learning (ML) models. LSMs and ESMs are process-based approaches which simulate fire occurrence and spread using parameterisations of vegetation, fuels, weather and ignitions, whereas statistical and ML approaches infer relationships between historical fire activity and environmental or socioeconomic drivers. Increasingly, hybrid frameworks combine elements of both approaches.These three approaches are summarised in Fig. 3, with further framework intercomparisons in section ‘Synthesis of modelling approaches’. The number of studies identified for each model type is summarised in Table S1 and all model acronyms are spelt out in Table S2.Fig. 3: Schematic representing the components of the different types of climate-fire models, and the options for coupling between model components.Full size imagePale colours indicate less routine processes, and dotted arrows are for less routine couplings/interactions. SLCF short-lived climate forcers.Land surface modelsLSMs are process-based models that simulate terrestrial vegetation structure, carbon cycling, and land-atmosphere exchanges. Most represent vegetation using plant functional types and include photosynthesis, stomatal conductance, vegetation dynamics, mortality, litter, soil decomposition and surface energy fluxes117,118,119,120. Some additionally include nitrogen cycling to constrain CO2 fertilisation responses.Many LSMs include explicit fire modules that simulate ignitions, fuel availability and moisture, fire spread, human suppression, burned area, fuel consumption and fire emissions121,122. These fire parametrisations may be embedded directly within the LSM118,123,124 or in a fire module that multiple LSMs can use74,125,126,127,128,129. LSMs require prescribed meteorology as input, or they can run online, coupled within an ESM (Section ‘Earth system models’). Major LSMs and their associated fire modules are summarised in Table S3.Recent LSM intercomparison projects, including TRENDY and FireMIP55,122,130,131,132,133, demonstrate substantial variability in simulated burned area and fire emissions. Interannual variability is frequently underestimated122,134,135. In FireMIP, this was attributed to models that did not capture the fuel buildup resulting from the vegetation productivity of previous seasons122.Historical evaluation is typically conducted against satellite-derived burned area and emissions datasets, including GFED, MODIS and FireCCI119,136,137,138,139. However, these observational products themselves contain considerable uncertainties (up to a factor of 3–5 globally)140,141,142,143. Advanced benchmarking frameworks, including ILAMB and AMBER124,144,145, and sensitivity experiments isolating drivers such as CO2, lightning, or population density139,144,146, are increasingly used to evaluate model behaviour and uncertainty. Models with improved representation of vegetation dynamics, agricultural burning and human suppression generally perform better against observations122,132. The treatment of fuel flammability and moisture is a large source of inter-model variability. Models estimate these quantities using proxies such as fire danger indices, vapour pressure deficit, soil moisture, relative humidity, temperature and precipitation139,147. Representation of agricultural burning also varies across models122,132, or is sometimes not included at all. Finally, biases in the climate models used to drive LSMs propagate directly into simulated fire behaviour136,148.Earth system modelsESMs simulate coupled interactions among the atmosphere, ocean, land and cryosphere. Future fire projections using ESMs generally fall into two categories: (1) prognostic simulations in which fires are explicitly simulated within coupled land-atmosphere frameworks (Table S3), and (2) studies that use ESM meteorological output to derive fire weather or fire risk indices (SI Note 3). The results from both types of studies are included in section ‘Modelling future fires under climate change’.Prognostic ESM fire simulations may be one-way or two-way coupled. In one-way coupled configurations, simulated meteorological fields drive fire occurrence and burned area, but the resulting fire emissions do not feed back onto the atmospheric system. In two-way coupled models, fire emissions are injected into the atmospheric component of the ESM, allowing interactions with atmospheric chemistry, aerosols, radiation, clouds and climate128,149,150,151,152 (Fig. 3). Most ESMs with prognostic fire modules are still one-way coupled, and model diversity remains limited. For example, in CMIP6, 19 ESMs submitted prognostic burned area or fire CO2 emissions, but these simulations were derived from only three primary fire modules embedded within nine LSMs153.Evaluation of ESMs also includes atmospheric concentrations of fire-emitted species, aerosol optical properties and wet and dry deposition. Community tools such as ESMValTool facilitate these comparisons using satellite and surface observational datasets154,155,156. ESM performance for the historical period has been evaluated for one-way coupled models in CMIP5 and CMIP6 intercomparison studies153,157,158, which demonstrated improvements relative to earlier model generations, attributed to advances in fire parameterisations and reductions in host-model climate biases153.Two-way coupled ESMs introduce additional complexity with explicit treatment of fire-emitted gases, aerosols, plume injection heights, atmospheric chemistry and aerosol-cloud interactions. Plume injection height is a particularly important component of the coupling process because it strongly influences aerosol lifetime, long-range transport and radiative forcing88. Emission speciation is derived from observationally constrained emission factors159,160 or parameterisations150 although they also remain highly uncertain a variable140,161,162,163.Although ESMs with prognostic fire capability have existed for more than a decade128,149,150,151,152,153, relatively few studies have applied fully coupled simulations to future wildfire projections.Statistical and machine learning modelsStatistical and ML models provide a data-driven alternative to process-based wildfire modelling. Rather than explicitly simulating physical fire processes, these approaches infer relationships between historical fire activity and environmental or socioeconomic drivers using observational datasets ranging from satellite-derived burned area to demographic indicators. Most statistical and ML frameworks rely on combinations of meteorological, vegetation, topographic and anthropogenic predictors164,165,166,167,168,169,170.As the availability of geospatial datasets has expanded, wildfire modelling has evolved from traditional regression relationships to ensemble and deep-learning frameworks capable of capturing non-linear interactions among climate, vegetation and human activity165,167,169,171,172,173,174,175. These models are increasingly used for wildfire prediction, fuel mapping, fire behaviour analysis and as diagnostic tools for identifying dominant controls on regional fire activity176. SI Note 2.1 and Table S4 contain more details on ML methods and types.Model evaluation is typically conducted against historical satellite-derived burned area and fire emissions datasets. Methods such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis are also increasingly used to improve interpretability and identify the dominant drivers of model behaviour177.Synthesis of modelling approachesFigure 3 summarises the three different modelling approaches for simulating or projecting fires in a changing climate, and their inter-connectivity. While both LSMs and ESMs are process-based, LSMs are less computationally expensive than fully-coupled ESMs. Despite continued improvements, both types of models still struggle to reproduce fire seasonality, interannual variability, extreme fire years, human interactions and regional fire distributions132,136,139,147,178,179. Important limitations include simplified ignition schemes based on climatological lightning or population density relationships36,119,120, coarse spatial resolution that under-represents small fires and fine-scale vegetation heterogeneity120,180,181, and incomplete representation of processes such as peat fires, tropical deforestation fires and multi-day fire persistence131,182.Each model type provides a complementary advantage and application. For example, two-way coupled ESMs provide the most complete and self-consistent representation of fire-climate interactions, allowing for climate-driven changes in fires183,184 (Figs. 1 and 3). However, due to the chaotic nature of the climate system and the stochastic nature of fire ignitions, they do not reproduce actual historical fires. Additionally, greater model complexity creates more opportunities for biases to accumulate. ESMs inherit limitations from their LSMs and also introduce additional biases in atmospheric variables48,185,186,187,188. However, ESMs driven by historically constrained BB emissions can well support detection and attribution studies. LSM simulations can be valuable for disentangling drivers of model diversity, and running the same LSM within several host ESMs can provide insights into the relative importance of host model climate153,157.Statistical and ML models are fundamentally different from ESMs and LSMs, though ML models are often trained from ESM and LSM output. Compared to process-based approaches, ML models are fast to run, taking advantage of the proliferation of potential input datasets. Comparisons between ML and process-based approaches remain relatively limited, though available studies demonstrate that ML models can outperform process-based models in reproducing historical burned area189 and PM2.5 emissions190.Statistical and ML models face several important limitations. Their performance depends strongly on the quality and representativeness of training datasets175,191. While projections from all model types are sensitive to biases in the underlying climate models, most ML frameworks do not explicitly enforce physical consistency, limiting their ability to simulate coupled Earth system responses164,167,192. These differences become most apparent when simulating compound fire-weather extremes, where fire behaviour depends on the simultaneous evolution of interacting meteorological and fuel variables. As these relationships may change under future climates, ML models trained on historical observations are less reliable when extrapolated beyond the range of past conditions than process-based models that explicitly represent the governing physical processes. Predictive skill also varies geographically, with lower performance often occurring in regions with complex topography or ecological transition zones193,194.Increasingly, hybrid ML-process approaches are being used to diagnose deficiencies in process-based fire models and improve future projections134,176. For example,176 used random forests to identify vegetation-fire interactions as a major source of uncertainty in global fire-enabled vegetation models. In addition, process-based and statistical models can be used as complementary tools in the same analyses, for example, in attribution studies linking anthropogenic climate change to increases in large fires70.For all modelling approaches, assessing historical performance is a prerequisite for reliable future projections. However, it is critical that models get the right answer for the right reasons, as the drivers of future trends may differ from those in the historical period, and models are tuned to present-day conditions. For instance, LSMs and ESMs sometimes fail to reproduce the observed decline in global burned area since 1850, and this was attributed to fire suppression and land use changes121,122,129,150,153,195. However, trends are already changing since the satellite era134,135,189,195,196, and these trends may continue to change in the future, via policies around deforestation and fire management. At the same time, CO2 fertilisation leads to enhanced vegetation growth and fuel load, and unprecedented warming will increase flammability. Representing regional differences in dominant fire drivers remains challenging. Evaluation based only on global metrics is dominated by tropical burning and can obscure poor performance in climatically sensitive regions such as boreal forests88,121,138,181.Despite limitations, process-based and ML models serve as useful frameworks for future fire projections135,153. Modern models extend beyond traditional ESM applications that provide meteorological data for estimating fire risk. They can support climate research and policy by examining the role of fire in future climates147,150,152, including the effects of changing fire emissions and land use management.Modelling future fires under climate changeHere, we provide a cross-framework synthesis of future projections of burned area, fire emissions, fire seasonality and fire risk from global and regional fire studies, with emphasis on end-of-century changes under CMIP climate scenarios183,197,198. Details on future scenarios are provided in SI Note 4. The results outlined below are broadly consistent with qualitative patterns across all model types, despite differences in methodology, though they do differ substantially in the magnitude of projected changes.Projected changes in future fire activityFigure 4 summarises projected future changes in global burned area and fire emissions from the literature across low-, moderate- and severe-warming scenarios. Despite large methodological differences among LSMs, ESMs and ML approaches, most studies project increasing global burned area and fire emissions by the late century, particularly under severe warming scenarios119,120,139,146,157,158,173,199,200.Fig. 4: Future vs present changes in fire activity.Full size imageBars indicate the projected percent change in global burned area (left) and fire emissions (right) relative to present-day conditions across low-, moderate- and severe-warming scenarios, synthesised from quantitative results in the literature (see Table S6 for details).The magnitude of projected changes varies greatly, partly due to differences in scenario definitions and averaging periods, but mainly because fire projections depend strongly on scenario choice, climate sensitivity, vegetation dynamics, human-fire interactions and model structure. MLs (e.g. from ref. 173) could project particularly strong increases under severe warming scenarios but may be sensitive to extrapolation beyond historical climate states. In contrast, some LSMs project weaker global increases or even regional declines where anthropogenic suppression, fragmentation, or reduced fuel availability offset climate-driven increases in fire weather144.Global fire carbon emissions are commonly projected to increase by roughly 50–100% under severe warming scenarios157,174,199,200. Lower-warming scenarios produce smaller changes or near-stabilisation of fire activity by late century119,158, although some studies still project increasing fire emissions201. Idealised CO2 experiments similarly suggest strong sensitivity of burned area and fire emissions to warming and CO2 fertilisation35,202.Coupled ESMs demonstrate that fire-emitted aerosols can influence regional temperature and precipitation through radiative and cloud effects88, highlighting an important advantage of fully interactive land-atmosphere modelling frameworks. However, few studies simultaneously include fully coupled fire aerosols, atmospheric chemistry and greenhouse gas feedbacks.Regional projections are summarised in Fig. 5. Across modelling frameworks, the clearest global signal is a strong poleward expansion and intensification of wildfire activity under climate warming4,120,200,203,204. These regions are projected to experience much longer fire seasons, more severe fire weather, increased lightning ignitions and large increases in burned area and fire emissions8,21,35,48,139,205,206,207,208,209,210,211. Burned area and fire carbon emissions may double or more under severe warming139,193,204,205,208,212.Fig. 5: Schematic synthesis of projected regional wildfire changes across modelling frameworks.Full size imageColours indicate the approximate magnitude and confidence of projected change, while arrows indicate modelling framework type (LSM = green, ESM = light blue, ESM-derived = dark blue, ML/statistical = orange). Dotted outlines indicate regions with particularly large inter-model uncertainty or disagreement (see Table S6 for details).In Canada, the annual burned area could increase to nearly five times the modern historical average by the 2090s under severe warming139. In China, a random forest ML approach projected increasing fire occurrence across 60–70% of forested regions by the late century, with large increases in burned area and an expansion of moderate- and high-risk zones213. Mediterranean ecosystems and western North America also emerge as major hotspots of increasing fire danger, with projections consistently showing more frequent heatwave- and drought-driven fire weather, larger fires and expanded fire seasons35,171,214,215,216. Southern Europe and the western United States may be especially vulnerable to increases in regional fire activity that could strain suppression capacity217,218,219. Under severe warming, burned area increases exceed 100% across parts of southern Europe165,171, and increases are significant even in a moderate warming scenario165,220.Projections for tropical regions are generally weaker, mixed, or declining120,137,167. Tropical and subtropical regions exhibit much greater divergence among projections and show greater regional variability. In parts of the Amazon, Cerrado and subtropical Africa, warming and drying are projected to increase fire probability, fire weather severity and ecosystem vulnerability, particularly where climate change interacts with deforestation and fragmentation35,199,221,222,223,224,225,226. However, most models project stable or declining burned area across portions of tropical Africa and South America because of reduced fuel availability, woody thickening, increasing precipitation, or enhanced human activity36,137,144,167,199,200,202,225,227,228. The changes can be mixed, with declining burned area across parts of northern hemispheric Africa but increasing fire activity across southern tropical South America under severe warming as in Li et al.167. The Congo Basin represents an example of methodological divergence, with some ESMs projecting declining fire activity associated with increased precipitation or reduced lightning ignitions48,88,229, while observation-constrained and ML approaches instead project enhanced fire emissions under intensified drying174,199. Even within individual studies, the projected sign of tropical fire changes can depend on methodological approach. For example, Yu et al.199 projected declining tropical fire emissions using direct ESM output, but increasing emissions when constraining the same simulations using ML techniques. The relative importance of hydrological sensitivity, CO2 fertilisation, vegetation change and human activity, therefore, remains highly uncertain across tropical ecosystems.Changes to fire behaviours and impactsFire seasons lengthen across northern mid-latitudes. Boreal and temperate fire seasons are projected to lengthen considerably35,48,119,226,230, often by one to 3 months21,137,148,206,211,214,231,232. In Fennoscandia, for example, the fire season may begin several weeks earlier and end up to 1 month later under severe warming211. Fire intensity also increases globally and regionally, from LSM and ML-based models. For example, using JSBACH-SPITFIRE, Veira et al.137 projected a 10–50% increase in the fraction of high-intensity fires under severe warming scenarios, and Dong et al.230, using a random forest ML model, simulated increases in large-fire days in southern California. Increasing biomass and burned area contribute to stronger smoke-related air quality impacts180,233,234. Several studies project increasing fire intensity and smoke exposure, such as large increases in wildfire PM2.5 concentrations and smoke-related health risks across boreal regions, the western United States, Latin America, Africa and Asia164,180,192,233,234,235.Many future wildfire studies derive fire weather or fire risk indices offline using ESM meteorological output rather than explicitly simulating fires. These approaches represent one of the earliest and most widely used methods for projecting future wildfire change50,236. Fire risk studies using ML models also exist. Most studies project pronounced increases in fire weather severity, fire-prone area and extreme fire conditions by the end of the 21st century4,21,219,237,238. Fire-prone conditions are projected to expand across much of the global burnable land surface238, with particularly large increases in boreal and temperate regions4,219. Extreme fire weather days are projected to double or triple in some regions21,217,219, while the duration of rare extreme fire events may increase considerably under severe warming232. Transitions toward higher fire-danger classifications will increase206,207,239, and significant increases in fire probability and fire risk are projected in Canada, China, Russia, the Mediterranean, the Alps, the western United States, and the Amazon170,213,218,222,240,241. Although fire-weather and fire-risk approaches focus primarily on meteorological drivers, several studies also identify important roles of land use, fuel connectivity and human activity215,222,240,242.Dominant drivers of fire changesProjected fire changes arise from interacting climatic, ecological and anthropogenic drivers, with projected fire change values differing considerably among regions because the dominant controls on fire activity vary geographically (Fig. 2). Several studies identify warming21,23,214,225,237,243 and drying as primary drivers of increasing fire activity119,202,226,233, while others emphasise the importance of CO2 fertilisation and increasing fuel availability35.In high-latitude regions including Canada, Siberia and Fennoscandia, increasing temperature, vapour pressure deficit and declining fuel moisture are consistently identified as dominant drivers of future fire increases4,35,120,139,158,202,207,211,229,237, with lightning ignition playing a significant role there as well139. Boreal regions are generally projected to remain moisture-limited, with warming-driven fuel drying dominating over fuel constraints211.Semi-arid regions such as the southwestern United States, the Brazilian Highlands, Australia and Central Asia are also projected to experience increasing fire risk associated with drying and increasing atmospheric moisture demand118,229, however, future fire activity remains strongly fuel-limited, making biomass availability and vegetation change particularly important35,202,239,244. Some studies emphasise the importance of fuel-limited versus moisture-limited fire regimes136,146. In parts of the Mediterranean, climate-driven drying may be partially offset by reduced net primary productivity and declining fuel availability136,146, and precipitation and CO2 fertilisation can increase fire risk by enhancing fine-fuel production202,216,237,239,244,245.Drivers in tropical regions are complex and result in differing future projections. Moist tropical regions remain especially sensitive to precipitation variability and drought occurrence216,229,245. In the Congo Basin, declining fire risk could be due to projected increases in precipitation229, whereas in tropical South America, there may be increasing fire activity and vegetation transitions under warming and drying226. In Mediterranean climates, Amazonia and southern Africa, future fire risk is strongly influenced by combined warming and drying trends215,246. Interpretable ML frameworks indicate that precipitation and vapour pressure deficit are dominant controls on tropical burned area variability167. Human influences remain important in some regions, increasing fire susceptibility in Chile247.Vegetation shifts also influence future fire behaviour. Increased CO2 can enhance vegetation productivity and fuel loads, particularly at high latitudes36,120,146, while woody encroachment in tropical savannahs may reduce grass-fuel continuity and suppress fire spread36,227. However, some LSMs simplify vegetation-fire feedbacks, potentially exaggerating some of these responses146, though inclusion of dynamic vegetation changes amplifies projected future burned area in the United States Liu and Wimberly192.Overall, the synthesis suggests a future global fire regime characterised by strong high-latitude amplification, intensifying fire-weather extremes across many temperate regions, and more uncertain but potentially transformative changes across tropical ecosystems4,120,203.Highlighting key uncertaintiesFuture fire projections remain highly uncertain across all modelling frameworks because fire activity depends on interacting climatic, ecological and anthropogenic processes that are themselves difficult to project under climate change. The dominant uncertainties limiting confidence in future projections are structural rather than parametric. Differences in future climate forcing and in the representation of vegetation, human activity and fire processes generally contribute more to projection spread than uncertainty in individual parameter values. Parameter uncertainty remains important, particularly for emissions, combustion and atmospheric chemistry, but typically has less influence on projected long-term changes in fire activity than structural differences among modelling frameworks (Table 1).Table 1 Sources of key uncertainties in fire modellingFull size tableOne of the largest sources of uncertainty originates from the climate models used to drive wildfire projections. LSM can exhibit up to a factor-of-five range in future fire emissions when driven by different climate models because differences in projected temperature and precipitation strongly influence vegetation productivity, fuel moisture and fuel availability148. Although ML approaches have improved historical fire simulations and attribution capabilities, they are also subject to climate forcing uncertainties. Divergence among driving ESMs remains a major limitation, with some studies showing disagreement in the direction of future fire-risk changes across more than half of land areas during the near term245. Consequently, ensemble weighting and Bayesian averaging approaches are increasingly used to reduce multi-model bias and improve projection robustness158,238.Projected fire responses may also strongly depend on the representation of moisture limitation and fuel drying. Allen et al.228 found that shortwave warming associated with aerosol reductions enhanced fuel drying more strongly than longwave greenhouse-gas warming. However, the sensitivity of these responses depends strongly on how fuel moisture constraints are represented, particularly in boreal regions where relative humidity may be a more important control on fire activity than soil moisture alone138,139.Lightning ignition is also a large uncertainty for fire projections, as different lightning parameterisations provide diverging projections185, and some models do not represent historical trends as compared to measurements44,47,50,210,225, greatly reducing confidence in their future projections. There is also no consensus on how much changing lightning will impact changes in global burned area. Its impact may be modest relative to fuel and climate effects200,202, or may be significant48,210,248. However, there is general agreement that lightning is a key driver of boreal fire variability120,139.Human activity introduces uncertainty and competing fire-influence that differs regionally and over time. There is parametric uncertainty through regionally varying impacts of population density on fire ignition and suppression144,148,153,157,179,227. These influences are particularly important in tropical and densely populated regions36,137,179,227, where factors such as agricultural expansion, urbanisation, landscape fragmentation and fire suppression have historically reduced burned area in many regions57, whereas escaped fires increasingly dominate burned area during extreme fire seasons249.Additional uncertainty arises from the historical datasets used to train and evaluate ML models. Satellite and reanalysis products can exhibit conflicting trends and extremes in fire-weather indices, propagating uncertainty into bias-correction and prediction frameworks250. Furthermore, many ML approaches rely on static vegetation and anthropogenic predictors that do not evolve dynamically with climate change, limiting their ability to capture future changes in fuel structure, vegetation composition and human infrastructure133,203. Although hybrid ML-process frameworks may help address some of these limitations (Section ‘Integrating AI with process-based models’), uncertainty increases under severe scenarios where future climate states diverge most strongly from the historical training record243. Regional sensitivities also vary. For example, projections across the European Alps are strongly influenced by uncertainties in lightning occurrence and precipitation seasonality170.Collectively, these uncertainties highlight the importance of multi-model ensembles, high-resolution downscaling, improved representation of dynamic vegetation and human-fire interactions, and tighter integration between process-based and data-driven modelling frameworks133. Uncertainties can also be well addressed via intercomparison projects.Insights from intercomparison studiesOlder intercomparison studies based on derived fire-weather indices revealed large uncertainties during the near term. Using fire indices derived from 16 ESMs, Moritz et al.245 found weak model agreement for projected fire activity changes during 2010–2039, with agreement strengthening by the late century as warming signals intensified. Bowman et al.178 emphasised the importance of dynamic vegetation-fire interactions and argued that fire-weather approaches alone are insufficient to capture coupled fire-climate feedbacks.At the time of writing, the only multi-model intercomparison study of future prognostic fires was Kloster and Lasslop157, who compared six CMIP5 ESMs with prognostic fire capability (nine model configurations total) for both the historical and future time periods. Their results demonstrated a divergence in projected future fire carbon emissions across models and scenarios (Fig. 6a–c), despite broad agreement toward increasing fire activity under stronger warming scenarios. This large inter-model spread reflects differences in climate sensitivity, vegetation responses, fire parameterisations and anthropogenic influences among ESMs.Fig. 6: CMIP5 and CMIP6 global fire emissions.Full size image(top row): Multi-model comparison of future fire carbon emissions from CMIP5 ESMs with prognostic fire capability under three climate scenarios: a RCP26 (low), b RCP45 (moderate) and c RCP85 (severe), from Kloster and Lasslop157 with permission. (bottom row) Projected future fire carbonaceous aerosol emissions, multi-model decadal averages from CMIP6 ESMs with prognostic fire capability, comparing simulations with climate-responsive fire feedbacks (left bars) and prescribed BB emissions (right bars). d For SSP126 (low), e SSP370 (severe) and f SSP585 (severe), from Whaley et al.252 with permission.No fully published intercomparison of prognostic future fires from CMIP6 ESMs is yet available. However, emerging analyses from CMIP6 models highlight an increasingly important distinction between prescribed and prognostic future fire emissions251,252,253. Prescribed CMIP BB emissions primarily reflect land-use changes, whereas prognostic simulations respond dynamically to changing climate, vegetation and weather conditions. Consequently, future fire emissions differ depending on whether fires are prescribed or interactively simulated (Fig. 6d–f).Intercomparison studies demonstrate the importance of ensemble approaches for quantifying projection uncertainty (e.g. ref. 254). For example, Cane et al.255 compared projections for an alpine region from a single regional climate model and a seven-model ensemble and found that the multi-model ensemble projected increases in fire potential and extreme fire-weather days, while the single-model simulation projected weaker or even opposite regional trends because of differences in precipitation responses. Thus, projections are sensitive to regional hydroclimate change, and multi-model approaches are generally more robust than individual simulations, particularly in regions with complex terrain and precipitation dynamics.Emerging opportunities and path forwardWhile future projections of fires are highly uncertain, given the strengths of each modelling approach, we summarise in Fig. 7 their best use cases. There are also several avenues that are recommended for a path forward, given how important reliable future fire projects are to society.Fig. 7: Summary of modelling approaches.Full size imageStructural components, and key take-away messages on their strengths, limitations and best use cases.Gaps in process-based modelsOne of the largest remaining gaps in wildfire modelling is the limited representation of two-way fire-climate feedback within ESMs (Section ‘Wildland fire controls on climate’). Although some studies now include fire-emitted aerosols and greenhouse gases256, most fire projections still neglect interactive impacts of chemistry, smoke-cloud interactions and atmospheric oxidative capacity. This omission may lead to systematic underestimation of long-term climate feedbacks from future fires. For example, Chen et al.86 incorporated gas-phase chemistry and found that future fire emissions substantially reduced atmospheric oxidative capacity, increasing methane concentrations to a similar magnitude as increasing wetland methane sources, and direct fire-related CO2 emissions.Current ESMs also incompletely represent longer-term cryosphere feedbacks associated with wildfire aerosols. While many models simulate black carbon deposition onto snow and ice surfaces257, they often neglect multi-year accumulation and persistence of deposited aerosols within Arctic snowpacks and glaciers. These long-memory effects may become increasingly important as accelerated polar warming exposes older snow and ice layers containing previously deposited fire-derived aerosols.Another major limitation is the treatment of fire persistence. Many LSMs and ESM fire modules simulate fires independently at daily timesteps and therefore cannot fully represent prolonged fire spread associated with large remote wildfires122. However, fire duration is a major control on burned area in regions such as boreal Canada212. Earlier approaches attempted to approximate persistence by linking fires across consecutive days258,259, while more recent studies have suggested using satellite-derived fire duration datasets to develop explicit fire-duration parameterisations132,260. A small number of LSMs now include multi-day fire behaviour182,261,262, however, these approaches have not yet been applied in future projection studies.Finally, peat fires are another important but incompletely represented process in global fire models. Peatlands have unique hydrological controls on fire occurrence and distinct fire-emission speciation263, while storing long-term carbon reservoirs that are increasingly vulnerable to warming and drying31,264,265. Despite peat fires being especially important in northern boreal and Arctic regions, which are warming faster than the global mean, they are not included in all global BB inventories140, and relatively few LSMs explicitly simulate peat fires. Notable exceptions include the Li fire scheme78,128,266 and INFERNO-peat267. Including and improving peat-fire representation will be essential for accurately projecting future carbon-cycle and climate feedbacks associated with high-latitude wildfire activity.Frameworks for coordinated multi-model studiesThe large diversity in fire metrics, regional definitions, scenarios, averaging periods and modelling frameworks currently limits direct comparison among future fire studies. Coordinated multi-model intercomparison frameworks are therefore essential for identifying robust emergent patterns, quantifying uncertainty and separating structural model differences from scenario-driven variability.Community efforts are increasingly addressing these challenges. FireMIP Phase 2 extends earlier historical intercomparisons toward future fire projections using multiple LSMs under consistent forcing scenarios133. Such coordinated experiments will provide important insight into the sources of uncertainty associated with vegetation dynamics, fuel representation, climate sensitivity and human-fire interactions across next-generation fire-enabled LSMs.The HTAP3 Fires project252 provides another framework for coordinated future fire experiments, including simulations using both prognostic fires from ESMs and prescribed future BB emissions that are climate sensitive253. HTAP3 Fires includes standardised regional definitions based on fire-biome characteristics, enabling more consistent comparison of burned area, emissions, atmospheric composition and fire-related climate impacts across modelling systems.Future CMIP7 activities are also expected to expand coordinated fire simulations. AerChemMIP2 will encourage ESMs with prognostic fire capability to provide historical and future scenario simulations268. CMIP7 additionally emphasise emissions-driven simulations, particularly for CO2, allowing more self-consistent representation of carbon-cycle feedbacks and improved assessment of Earth system responses and potential climate tipping points184,269,270.These coordinated project provide an important pathway toward more robust, comparable and policy-relevant future fire projections.Integrating AI with process-based modelsHybrid approaches that integrate ML with process-based models are a promising direction for improving future fire projections and reducing computational limitations. For example, Kavhu et al.134 developed a statistical burned-area model designed for coupling with LSMs, using generalised linear models to represent relationships among biophysical and socioeconomic drivers simulated within process-based frameworks.Fire plume rise and in-plume atmospheric chemistry, which forms secondary organic aerosol and ozone and involves non-linear interactions that are computationally expensive to simulate using traditional parameterisations, can be replaced with ML approaches that provide efficient surrogate frameworks trained on high-fidelity simulations or observations172,207. Such approaches could reduce computational costs while retaining sensitivity to evolving meteorological and fire conditions. Faster emulators are also highlighted for their potential in long-term planning and identifying locations with higher future fire danger162,271.Given that process-based models exhibit systematic biases associated with fire emission factors, plume injection heights, atmospheric chemistry and aerosol processes, residual-learning frameworks can identify persistent discrepancies between model output and observations and apply statistical corrections to improve air-quality forecasts158,172,207,230,248.Another emerging direction is physics-informed ML, which embeds physical constraints directly within ML architectures272. Unlike purely black-box AI approaches, these hybrid frameworks incorporate conservation laws, chemical stoichiometry and biophysical constraints into neural-network training. Such approaches may help preserve physical consistency while improving predictive capability under future climate conditions. Hybrid ML-physics frameworks can accelerate computationally intensive components of atmospheric chemistry models174, enabling rapid sensitivity analyses of fire-driven atmospheric composition changes.AI-based inference approaches may also improve representation of poorly observed fire processes, including fuel moisture variability, ignition probability and human-fire interactions derived from multidimensional observational datasets248,272. By combining physically-based process understanding with adaptive data-driven inference, hybrid frameworks provide a potentially powerful pathway toward more flexible, computationally efficient and observationally-constrained fire projections under future climate change.Toward actionable fire-climate projectionsAs wildfire models become increasingly complex, improving interpretability and societal relevance is becoming an important priority. Explainable AI frameworks, including SHAP, are being used to diagnose why models predict heightened fire activity and to identify dominant environmental and anthropogenic drivers207,248. Such approaches may improve confidence in wildfire projections and help translate increasingly complex modelling systems into information that is more actionable for decision-makers and fire managers.There is also growing demand for high-resolution, user-oriented fire projections at spatial scales relevant to local adaptation and management rather than global or continental averages133,158,172,181,250. Future wildfire assessments will increasingly require improved representation of extreme fire behaviour, including prolonged fire-conducive weather patterns, compound extremes and the heavy-tailed nature of rare fire seasons that are often smoothed within monthly or climatological averages165,175,273.Human-fire interactions remain a research priority and opportunity. Ignition sources, fire suppression, land management and socioeconomic development all strongly influence future fire trajectories and could be better represented in models73,224,245,274,275. For example, incorporating the Human Development Index into an LSM may better represent suppression capacity over time195,276. Scenario-based fire-management pathways were developed for Arctic states277 and could provide a promising framework for future modelling experiments that provide policy-relevant results.Despite marked advances in wildfire modelling over recent decades, major uncertainties remain in projecting future fire activity. There is broad agreement across model frameworks that climate change will increase fire risk and extreme fire activity in many regions, particularly in the extra-tropics and boreal forests, although large variations persist in the magnitude of these changes. Future progress will depend on improved representation of coupled fire-climate-human interactions. Each model framework provides complementary information, though emerging hybrid approaches that integrate process-based modelling, observations and explainable ML provide a promising path toward more robust and actionable fire projections across spatial scales relevant to both Earth system science and decision-making.

items.title: Clima, agosto 2026 il più caldo della storia
items.description:
Agosto 2026 è stato il mese piu' caldo mai registrato sulla Terra, alla pari con luglio 2023,
The post Clima, agosto 2026 il più caldo della storia ap
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie WWF: “I dati diffusi da Copernicus dovrebbero mobilitare i governi del Pianeta” Agosto mai così caldo da quando si misurano le temperature medie terrestri. Dopo nove mesi, la temperatura globale sale oltre la soglia di 1,5 gradi rispetto all’epoca preindustriale. La temperatura media globale dell’aria superficiale ha raggiunto 16,96 gradi centigradi, 0,85 gradi sopra la media 1991-2020 e 1,65 gradi sopra quella stimata per il periodo preindustriale 1850-1900. A rilevarlo è il Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), implementato dal Centro europeo per le previsioni meteorologiche a medio termine (ECMWF), nel nuovo bollettino climatico mensile. Agosto 2026 è stato il primo mese a superare nuovamente la temperatura media globale di 1,5 gradi centigradi dal novembre 2025. In Europa, gran parte delle regioni occidentali e meridionali hanno registrato temperature sopra la media, con un +3°C di Francia e Italia.  Il dato non riguarda soltanto l’atmosfera. Nell’agosto 2026 la temperatura superficiale media degli oceani, tra 60 gradi Sud e 60 gradi Nord, ha superato i 21°C: è il valore più alto mai osservato per agosto e gli scienziati rilevano che le temperature record per mari e oceani si sono protratte per oltre tre mesi. La crisi climatica sta portando il Pianeta e suoi abitanti verso territori nuovi e potenzialmente molto pericolosi. Già oggi sta producendo fenomeni estremi nell’atmosfera e negli oceani, con impatti sempre più evidenti nelle comunità, nelle economie e negli ecosistemi di tutto il mondo. Questi dati dovrebbero spingere i Governi di tutto il mondo ad agire insieme e in fretta, dovrebbe indurre tutti a mettere la crisi climatica in cima alle priorità. WWF Italia In Europa caldo e siccità, allarme fiumi in secca In Europa il caldo è stato accompagnato da una siccità molto estesa, dalla Gran Bretagna all’Europa Meridionale . Ad agosto condizioni più secche della media hanno interessato alcune aree dell’Europa occidentale e vaste regioni dell’Europa centrale e orientale. I suoli superficiali hanno raggiunto livelli di umidità eccezionalmente bassi nelle zone colpite dalla siccità, mentre aridità e incendi hanno interessato diverse regioni del continente. Particolarmente significativo il segnale proveniente dai maggiori fiumi europei: Danubio e Reno hanno registrato portate eccezionalmente basse. come anche Vistola, Rodano, Senna. In Italia Po e Sesia sono ai minimi storici. Il questionario “Senti già la crisi climatica?” Il WWF Italia invita i cittadini a far emergere il peso dell’impatto dei fenomeni climatici sulla propria vita. Per aiutarli, l’associazione ha promosso, con il sostegno del Movimento Laudato Si’ e altre realtà civiche, un’indagine partecipata per analizzare l’impatto concreto della crisi climatica sulla vita quotidiana della popolazione. Senti già la crisi climatica? items.description: Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta Proponiamo il primo di una serie di post dedicata ad uno degli imp
items.body:
Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta                
												
																																	                
					Ago 31, 2026Ago 31, 20262 commenti su Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta

Clima e incendi: 1- L’incendio di Eaton Canyon a Los Angeles e la tempesta perfetta

Proponiamo il primo di una serie di post dedicata ad uno degli impatti più immediati e devastanti del riscaldamento climatico: gli incendi. Cominciamo col presentare un evento estremo, uno dei due incendi principali che hanno interessato Los Angeles nel gennaio 2025. Innescato nei pressi di un traliccio dell’alta tensione sulle montagne nei pressi di Eaton Canyon, quest’incendio ha devastato un vastissimo versante montuoso e la cittadina di Altadena, distruggendo in poche ore circa 10,000 strutture abitative e commerciali. Un incendio questo verificatosi in seguito alla successione di una siccità di otto mesi ed un intenso evento ventoso di Santa Ana cominciato il 7 gennaio 2025. Un caso più unico che raro o una concreta possibilità anche altrove, oggi o in futuro?

Figura 1: Le fiamme dell’incendio innescato nei pressi di Eaton Canyon avvolgono alcune abitazioni di Altadena in California l’8 gennaio 2025.

Nella notte dell’8 gennaio 2025, i 43,000 abitanti di Altadena, una cittadina a ridosso delle montagne a est di Los Angeles in California, si trovarono a prendere nel giro di qualche minuto una delle decisioni più importante della loro vita.

Durante l’anno precedente (2024), quest’area della California del Sud era stata interessata da un inverno piuttosto piovoso a cui era seguita una siccità pressoché continua durante il resto dell’anno. La successione di un periodo più piovoso del solito ed uno molto arido aveva sviluppato sui ripidi pendii montuosi sovrastanti Altadena una rigogliosa vegetazione arbustiva che, risecchitasi poi durante un periodo siccitoso di 8 mesi, era andata a costituire un significativo accumulo di biomassa potenzialmente combustibile.

La mattina del 7 gennaio 2025 un evento ventoso, riconducibile ai tipici venti di Santa Ana (venti secchi di ricaduta provenienti dalle zone desertiche continentali), cominciò ad interessare le montagne a ridosso di Altadena in maniera molto intensa. Le raffiche di vento arrivarono ad una velocità di 130-160 km/h paragonabili, per dare un’idea, alla forza della tempesta Vaia che nell’autunno del 2018 devastò parte dei boschi delle Alpi Orientali Italiane.

La sera del 7 gennaio 2025 le fiamme si svilupparono dapprima tra i secchi arbusti di macchia mediterranea nei pressi di Eaton Canyon, appena sopra Altadena. Il luogo d’innesco stava proprio al di sotto di un traliccio dell’alta tensione, come riscontrato da videocamere puntate in quella direzione da valle. Un video mostra infatti come quella sera si siano formati degli archi elettrici su un traliccio, probabilmente a causa delle forti raffiche di vento, con conseguente ricaduta di scintille sul terreno sottostante.

Figura 2: Immagine satellitare della cittadina di Altadena quasi completamente avvolta dalle fiamme l’8 gennaio 2025.

A quel punto il fuoco, alimentato dalla diffusa presenza di arbusti secchi e dalle forti raffiche di vento, divenne inarrestabile. Senza che i mezzi aerei antincendio potessero intervenire a causa della tempesta di vento e senza che le squadre di pompieri potessero fronteggiare direttamente le molteplici fiamme a causa del loro vasta diffusione e del calore intensissimo, l’incendio si propagò in poche ore su gran parte del versante montuoso. Dapprima il fuoco procedette da nord verso sud, per poi invertire direzione durante la notte e propagarsi anche tra le abitazioni di Altadena (Fig. 2), in seguito ad una “pioggia” di braci incandescenti trasportate dal vento che agirono da molteplice innesco (spotting) tra le dense abitazioni in legno ed i giardini ricchi di vegetazione ornamentale della cittadina. Uno studio recente relativo agli incendi di Los Angeles ha mostrato come la densità delle strutture sia stato un fattore critico nel causare la distruzione degli edifici durante l’incendio, forse ancora più importante della copertura arborea urbana di cui era ricca Altadena.

Nella notte dell’8 gennaio gli abitanti di Altadena ricevettero un SMS da parte delle autorità che diedero in questo modo l’ordine di evacuazione immediato. La quasi totalità della popolazione abbandonò in pochi minuti le proprie abitazioni, salvando la propria vita ma lasciando al loro destino le abitazioni rimaste senza un presidio che potesse contrastare anche solo molteplici piccoli inneschi causati delle braci trasportate dal vento. In molti casi, una volta penetrato all’interno degli edifici, il fuoco poté svilupparsi rapidamente, fino anche all’accensione quasi simultanea dei materiali combustibili interni (flashover). Da quel momento le case in fiamme diventarono a loro volta sorgenti di calore molto intenso e, generando nuove braci, propagarono il fuoco alle case circostanti. In questo modo circa 10,000 strutture abitative e commerciali di Altadena vennero completamente distrutte (Fig. 3).

Figura 3: La cittadina di Altadena quasi completamente devastata nei giorni immediatamente successivi all’incendio.

L’8 gennaio 2025 le vittime ad Altadena furono 19, una perdita drammatica ma un numero relativamente ridotto per un evento di tali dimensioni, grazie soprattutto alla rapida ed efficiente esecuzione della procedura di evacuazione della popolazione. Dopo aver distrutto gran parte degli edifici di Altadena, nei giorni successivi l’incendio si propagò sui versanti montuosi sovrastanti per 25 km fino a 2000 metri di quota interessando un’area totale di 5674 ettari prima di essere contenuto dai mezzi aerei antincendio entrati finalmente in azione dopo la cessazione delle intense raffiche di vento di Santa Ana.

Quella notte dell’8 gennaio in pochi minuti la comunità di Altadena si era stata salvata ma allo stesso tempo era anche stata sradicata dal suo territorio, senza una concreta possibilità di ritorno a breve termine e, in molti casi, anche a lungo termine. In seguito, il 5% degli abitanti hanno deciso infatti di vendere quello che restava delle loro proprietà, una volta bonificate dalle macerie e dalle ceneri delle case distrutte dall’incendio. L’incendio, distruggendo le abitazioni e strutture, aveva di fatto reso disponibili nuovi terreni edificabili per il mercato e la speculazione edilizia.

Per comprendere questa conseguenza, forse inaspettata, è necessario considerare il contesto attuale dell’edilizia abitativa in California: in breve mancano case e quindi la domanda è di gran lunga superiore all’offerta. Le cause di questo fenomeno sono ben spiegate nel libro di Francesco Costa, “California fine del sogno” ma sostanzialmente alcune leggi californiane di protezione ambientale sono state usate per impedire la costruzione di nuove case popolari per non diminuire il valore delle singole abitazioni adiacenti. L’incendio del Gennaio 2025 ha scombinato questa situazione di stallo ad Altadena ed ha dato il via libera alla costruzione di nuove case, più moderne e probabilmente con più appartamenti. Oggi un lotto di terreno completamente bruciato vale una cifra dell’ordine di mezzo milione di dollari ad Altadena mentre due terzi dei lotti effettivamente venduti sono stati acquistati da investitori. Tuttavia, la ricostruzione non sta procedendo velocemente: un rapporto indica che nove mesi dopo l’incendio 7 abitazioni gravemente danneggiate su 10 non mostravano ancora alcun segno di progresso verso la ricostruzione, in particolare le case di proprietari afroamericani e asiatici, maggiormente esposti a problemi di accesso alle risorse necessarie e al fenomeno della sottoassicurazione.

Impossibile quantificare precisamente l’enorme danno economico e morale sofferto da Altadena e dai suoi abitanti. Tuttavia il fondo californiano di assicurazione per gli incendi ha pagato fino ad ora 22367 richieste di risarcimento (su un totale di 22890) per danni a proprietà residenziali ($ 7.39 miliardi , inclusi i danni anche per solo inquinamento da fumi); 1079 (su 1262) a proprietà commerciali ($ 532 milioni) e 3392 (su 3814) a auto private e commerciali ($ 62 milioni). Un bilancio grave per le assicurazioni che tuttavia non avranno probabilmente particolari problemi ad assicurare le nuove abitazioni che verranno realizzate con materiali ignifughi e saranno protette da sistemi e procedure antincendio adeguate. L’8 gennaio del 2025 Altadena è bruciata anche perché dal cielo pioveva letteralmente fuoco su vecchie case di legno.

Di fronte a tale devastazione viene da chiedersi: ma l’incendio che ha distrutto gran parte di Altadena è risultato in seguito ad una successione di eventi (una lunga siccità e l’intenso evento ventoso di Santa Ana) che sono possibili solo nella California del Sud? E questo incendio è stato il risultato prevedibile di eventi che si erano già presentati nel passato? E non ultimo, i cambiamenti climatici in corso hanno avuto un ruolo nel determinare i fattori scatenanti l’incendio, ovvero la lunghissima siccità e l’intenso evento ventoso di Santa Ana?  Cercare di rispondere a queste domande è importante per cominciare a capire se eventi come questo siano potenzialmente riproducibili in altre zone del pianeta oggi oppure in futuro.  Questo è l’argomento che tratteremo nel prossimo post dedicato agli incendi.

items.title: Un altro grafico fuorviante su La Verità per disinformare sul clima
items.description: Il 2 agosto su “La Verità” è uscito un ennesimo articolo di disinformazione sul cambiamento climatico, firmato da Franco Battaglia, che contiene alcun
items.body:
Un altro grafico fuorviante su La Verità per disinformare sul clima                
												
																																	                
					Ago 23, 2026Ago 30, 20262 commenti su Un altro grafico fuorviante su La Verità per disinformare sul clima

Il 2 agosto su “La Verità” è uscito un ennesimo articolo di disinformazione sul cambiamento climatico, firmato da Franco Battaglia, che contiene alcune fandonie, per certi aspetti originali nel panorama del negazionismo climatico. Errori e travisamenti talmente clamorosi da sembrare per certi aspetti anche divertenti. In sostanza, Battaglia mostra una ricostruzione delle temperature che si ferma prima della rivoluzione industriale, per affermare che gli aumenti osservati a partire dalla stessa non sono rilevanti.

Un refrain trito e ritrito del negazionismo climatico è quello secondo cui il clima sarebbe sempre cambiato, per cui non dovremmo preoccuparci delle attuali grandi variazioni.

Per ribadire questa tesi, in passato Franco Battaglia ha usato grafici sbagliati (si veda il precedente post), frutto di errori o di vere e proprie manomissioni. Questa volta invece il grafico è reale, ma è stato usato senza capirlo, facendogli dire il contrario di quello che in realtà dice.

Secondo Battaglia, il grafico (pubblicato qui a fianco) descrive “il clima del pianeta corso degli ultimi 10.000 anni, derivato dai carotaggi in Groenlandia. All’estrema destra della figura ci siamo noi, ove l’ultima parte del grafico, la caccola di riscaldamento dentro il cerchio rosso, sarebbe quello che toglie il sonno agli sprovveduti”.

In realtà in questo grafico, derivante dai carotaggi nel progetto Greenland Ice Sheet Project 2 (GISP2), la parte più a destra, lo zero che descrive il punto di partenza del conteggio degli “anni prima del presente”, è relativo al… 1855! Il grafico si ferma infatti a 95 anni “prima del presente”, dove per presente si intende il 1950, una convenzione nel mondo della ricerca paleoclimatica del tempo (si veda qui per i dettagli). Manca pertanto proprio il cambiamento delle temperature degli ultimi 170 anni, successivo all’utilizzo su larga scala dei combustibili fossili, un aumento di oltre un grado centigrado.

Il circoletto evidenziato da Battaglia, l’aumento di due decimi di grado, è avvenuto nel diciottesimo e diciannovesimo secolo, tra il 1690 e il 1855, nei dati originali; pertanto non si tratta affatto del “riscaldamento attuale”, “quello che toglie il sonno ai catastrofisti climatici”.

Per far capire l’entità dell’ennesima cantonata presa da Battaglia, abbiamo riprodotto il grafico citato, riferendo per leggibilità la scala temporale agli anni del calendario, e accanto ai dati dei carotaggi abbiamo aggiunto (in rosso) le misure delle temperature recenti, fino al 2024, della stessa zona della Groenlandia, prese dal dataset BEST, raccolto ed elaborato all’università di Berkeley, e mediate su intervalli di 10 anni per renderle confrontabili.

Figura 1: Temperatura del carotaggio GISP-2 (blu) con aggiunti i dati di temperatura dal dataset BEST relativi al punto di griglia 72.5N, -38.5, il più vicino alle coordinate del carotaggio GISP-2  (72.583N, -38.466).

Possiamo quindi notare come già nell’ultimo decennio le temperature fossero vicine a quelle dei periodi precedenti, e come l’incremento sia rapidissimo, maggiore rispetto agli eventi passati, e tale da rendere molto più difficile l’adattamento degli ecosistemi e delle specie viventi.

Il confronto comunque ha poco senso. Quelle di GISP sono ricostruzioni delle temperature relative ad un singolo punto della Groenlandia; sebbene Battaglia le presenti come indicatrici delle temperature globali, l’andamento è specifico di quel sito, e risente di fattori locali. Una slavina può alterare localmente la sequenza degli strati, e il sito ha variato la sua elevazione nel periodo considerato (e una differenza di quota altera la temperatura). Pur se sono dati importanti per ricostruire la storia climatica passata, i dati di un singolo luogo non possono che descrivere fluttuazioni locali, diverse da quelle dell’intera Groenlandia.

Anche solo per ricostruire la storia climatica della Groenlandia gli studiosi hanno quindi effettuato numerosi altri carotaggi, in modo da ridurre l’effetto di queste fluttuazioni. Ne emerge un quadro in cui effettivamente in passato, intorno a 6000 anni BC, la Groenlandia ha avuto un clima leggermente più caldo dell’attuale, ma con variazioni molto lente, e senza i picchi pronunciati che Battaglia identifica con i periodi caldi minoico, romano e medioevale. Con il tasso di emissioni di gas serra il riscaldamento attuale è comunque destinato a superare nel giro di un decennio anche questo massimo. In figura 2 è mostrata questa ricostruzione, assieme alle misure di temperatura attuale nei siti dei carotaggi (attualmente circa 2°C nella scala indicata).

Figura 2: Ricostruzione delle temperature in Groenlandia negli ultimi 12.000 anni, da Vinther et al, Nature (2009). In nero la media delle temperature nei siti di carotaggio, fino al 2014 (dal sito www.carbonbrief.org).

Per quanto decisamente più rappresentative, si tratta ancora di ricostruzioni locali. Le variazioni delle temperature in piccole aree del pianeta sono inevitabilmente soggette a maggiori fluttuazioni rispetto alle temperature mediate su tutto il globo, e le alte latitudini, in particolare, sono molto sensibili a piccole variazioni di insolazione. Infatti, se si guardano le ricostruzioni delle temperature medie globali (figura 3), è possibile constatare come le fluttuazioni nel periodo considerato siano molto minori, e più lente, di quanto il grafico della Groenlandia riporti, e come l’attuale riscaldamento (che, anche qui, è proseguito dopo la realizzazione di quel grafico)  sia senza precedenti negli ultimi 24000 anni della storia climatica del pianeta. Emerge ancora in modo chiarissimo la grandissima anomalia delle variazioni recenti delle temperature.

Figura 3: Ricostruzione di temperatura globale degli ultimi 12000 anni con metodi differenti (linee colorate) presa da Kaufman et al. 2020. In grigio sono mostrati i percentili 5-95 di ogni ricostruzione e di quella complessiva. In nero i dati di rianalisi (ERA-20C) relativi all’ultimo secolo.

Quindi in sostanza si tratta dell’ennesima falsificazione di informazioni scientifiche a proprio uso e consumo, l’esatto opposto di quello che il metodo e l’etica scientifici prevedono.

Testo di Gianni Comoretto, con contributi di Roberto Ingrosso, Stefano Caserini e Mario Grosso.

Segnalo a chi fa divulgazione climatica il terribile video della distruzione della dogana cinese, nell’attuale disastro in Nepal, causato da un enorme distacco glaciale (10 mil. di metri cubi di ghiaccio, precipitati di colpo per 1400 metri), con ogni probabilità favorito dall’aumento in quota delle temperature (il giorno prima era sta notata nell’area, la scomparsa della neve che copriva il ghiacciaio, fusa e finita a fare da lubrificante sotto la massa ghiacciata)
Nel video si vedono centinaia di uomini piccoli come formiche che corrono disperatamente di fronte alla massa di acqua e roccia che si avvicina. Ma è tutto inutile, la sua potenza è spaventosa, solleva un intero parcheggio pieno di camion e autobus e lo scaglia come un giocattolo contro il fianco della montagna, e  poi cancella tutto il resto. E’ una immagine che ci dovremmo scolpire nella mente, perchè il suo simbolismo è evidente, profetico: è quello che ci accadrà a livello planetario, se non bloccheremo sul serio il cambiamento climatico.
